blocks.heading: The four connected functions
blocks.text: Planning sets objectives and chooses how to achieve them. Organising allocates people, tasks and other resources. Leading guides and motivates people so they understand and work towards the objectives. Controlling compares results with standards and initiates corrective action. These functions form a connected cycle rather than four isolated jobs. A manager plans a delivery deadline, organises the required staff and materials, explains priorities and supports the team, then checks progress and corrects a shortage. Feedback from control can change the next plan. Managers often perform several functions during one conversation, so classify the action described rather than the manager’s job title. Checking a result is control; choosing the future target is planning. A manager’s personal honesty is a quality supporting these functions, not a fifth function.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Luma Bags must fill a school order. Its manager sets a completion date, assigns cutting and sewing work, explains quality requirements and compares completed bags with the schedule. Setting the date is planning; assigning tasks is organising; guiding the team is leading; comparing progress is controlling. If sewing falls behind, the manager should investigate and reallocate resources if appropriate, linking control back to organisation and planning.

blocks.heading: Planning
blocks.text: Planning sets objectives and decides how resources and actions will achieve them. A useful plan states the intended result, timing, responsibilities and assumptions. It can reduce avoidable uncertainty, although forecasts cannot remove every risk. Plans should be revised when evidence changes rather than followed mechanically.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Awa Tiles estimates demand and schedules materials for next month’s output. Choosing the future target and how to meet it is planning. Counting what was actually completed belongs to control.

blocks.heading: Organising
blocks.text: Organising arranges people, tasks, authority and resources to carry out plans. It clarifies responsibilities and coordinates contributions so that required work is neither duplicated nor omitted. A plan for increased output is ineffective if materials and staff are unavailable at the right time. Organising is an activity; an organisation chart is one tool for showing the resulting responsibilities.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Karo Furniture allocates cutting, sanding and assembly tasks and ensures tools are available. Matching the people and tools to these tasks is organising. Merely announcing the target does not make those resources available.

blocks.heading: Leading
blocks.text: Leading guides, communicates with and motivates people towards business objectives. It includes explaining priorities, listening to difficulties and supporting coordinated effort. It is more than issuing orders: people need to understand the task and have the means to perform it. The most suitable approach depends on staff, urgency and risk.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nima Meals’ supervisor explains why allergen checks matter and listens to a worker’s concern about unclear labels. Guidance and listening support correct action and shared understanding. The supervisor should resolve the label problem rather than assuming motivation alone removes it.

blocks.heading: Controlling
blocks.text: Controlling sets or uses performance standards, measures actual results, compares them with the standard and takes corrective action where needed. It is not simply punishing staff or checking attendance. Investigating causes matters because the same shortfall can arise from different problems. Feedback can lead to revised plans, different resource allocation or clearer guidance.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Ova Prints compares actual spoiled sheets with its quality target and finds an equipment fault. Repairing the fault addresses the cause. Blaming the operator without investigating would not be effective control.
